html:
The map's label for the peoples of the Amazon rainforest, shown from 1500 BCE to 1783. The label undersells them: most Amazonian peoples farmed as well as hunting and fishing, and some built large settled societies.

How people lived:

  • fishing in the rivers and in floodplain lakes, the richest source of food;
  • hunting monkeys, peccary and tapir with bows, blowguns and traps;
  • gathering fruit, palm hearts and Brazil nuts;
  • clearing small gardens to grow manioc, first bred in south-western Amazonia by early manioc farmers, along with peppers, peach palm and other crops.

Over centuries people made dark, fertile soils, terra preta, from charcoal, pottery and waste, which are still farmed today. On Marajó island at the river mouth, the Marajoara culture built mounds and made painted pottery for about a thousand years. Earthworks in Acre and Bolivia show other large societies.

In 1542 the Spaniard Francisco de Orellana sailed down the whole river and reported many large settlements along its banks. Later travellers found few, probably because European diseases had spread ahead of them. Arawak, Carib and Tupi languages spread widely across the basin.

After 1600 Portuguese slave raids, Jesuit missions and epidemics struck again and again, and the rubber boom of the late 1800s brought forced labour. Many Amazonian peoples survive, some still living without contact with the outside world.
